area_title: ASP.NET Core filters main theory: pipeline, ordering, exception handling, DI, factories, result/status behavior
what_area_is_about: where MVC filters sit relative to middleware and endpoint/action execution
sync vs async filter forms and before/after execution nesting
filter ordering and how ordered filters wrap each other
exception filters, handled exception propagation, and why they cannot catch earlier authorization/resource failures
dependency injection for filters: global filters, TypeFilter, ServiceFilter, filter attributes, services from HttpContext
IFilterFactory and passing values from attributes while still constructing service-backed filters
status-code pages vs MVC/result filters, ObjectResult/content negotiation, ViewResult error pages, invalid model-state response customization
key_ideas: Middleware is the outer pipeline; MVC filters run inside endpoint/MVC execution and can reason about actions, models, results, and MVC context.
Async filters are usually preferred when a filter performs asynchronous work; they wrap the next delegate and can run before and after it.
Filter ordering matters because each filter wraps later stages; after-code runs on unwind, so mental model should be nested rather than flat.
Exception filters can mark an exception handled and stop propagation, but they do not catch exceptions thrown before their stage, such as authorization-filter failures.
Plain attributes are metadata and should not be treated as normal DI-created services; TypeFilter/ServiceFilter/global filters/IFilterFactory solve different DI and argument-passing cases.
Result filters are useful when handling MVC results and content negotiation; generic status-code pages are lower-level and may not have enough MVC/action context.
The region is theory-heavy and intentionally leaves concrete filter-type examples for R02 and lower middleware reminder/addendum for R03.
